newsitem.title: GERMANY: Rexrodt sees chance for German shopping on Sundays.
newsitem.headline: Rexrodt sees chance for German shopping on Sundays.

text.p: German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, claiming new liberalised shop-hour laws were a success, said on Saturday that he expected German shops to be allowed to open on Sundays by the turn of the century.
Rexrodt said in a commentary in Germany's Bild am Sonntag newspaper that the new shop-hour laws, which took effect on November 1, proved to be successful during the Christmas holiday shopping period.

Bonn extended Germany's shopping laws in November to allow stores to remain open until 8 p.m. on weekdays and generally until 4 p.m. on Saturdays. But shops must still remain closed on public holidays and on Sundays.

Rexrodt said retailers would likely be able to open their stores on Sundays by the year 2000, if they wished to do so, particularly since so many Germans visited many stores on Sunday that are open for viewing but not for sales.
"Such nonsense will certainly soon come to an end," Rexrodt said of the policy allowing stores to open their doors on Sundays but not to sell goods or services.
"In 2000, we should be allowed to buy more than just bread on Sundays. Goverment policies must reflect the wishes of the public and shop-hour times must become more flexible," he said.
But the HDE German retail federation said on Saturday that the controversial liberalisation in shop hours had done little to boost sagging retail sales and only added costs.
HDE leader Holger Wenzel told the Cologne newspaper "Express" that one-third of German retailers were unsatisfied with the new shop hours.
Wenzel also said he expected some shops to shorten their shop hours after a two-month trial period ends, saying consumers responded slowly to the additional shopping hours, particularly on Saturdays.
